summary: Describes Packet Ordering Function (POF) algorithms for Deterministic Networking. Replicating and eliminating packets in DetNet can deliver packets out of order, which time-sensitive applications cannot accept. POF restores the correct order, but only within the latency bound of the flow.

plainLanguage.summary: If you mail a book's pages by two routes, they may arrive shuffled. This explains how to put the pages back in order before handing them over.

questions: how does packet ordering work in detnet
when do packets arrive out of order
what is the packet ordering function
subtitle: Restoring packet order in deterministic networks

tldr.problem: When Deterministic Networking uses replication and elimination to protect against packet loss, packets can arrive out of order. Some time-sensitive applications cannot tolerate this.
tldr.mechanism: The Packet Ordering Function (POF) buffers out-of-order packets and releases them in sequence, respecting the flow's latency bounds.
tldr.outcome: Applications receive packets in the correct order. POF does not guarantee delivery or reduce delay, but restores order within the flow's latency bounds.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: Restore packet order after replication and elimination

facts.label: What it does NOT provide
facts.value: Reliability, duplicate detection, or error correction

today: RFC 9550 is an Informational RFC describing the algorithms for packet ordering in Deterministic Networking. It does not define a standard track specification but provides implementation guidance for DetNet systems that use packet replication and elimination.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) uses a Packet Replication Function (PRF) and Packet Elimination Function (PEF) to protect against packet loss. The PRF sends the same packet over multiple paths; the PEF receives them and discards duplicates, keeping one copy. This protection strategy works well for reliability, but it can result in packets arriving at the receiving end out of order.

Some applications, especially industrial systems and real-time control, cannot tolerate out-of-order packets. A single out-of-order packet might be treated as an error; multiple out-of-order packets in a row can trigger a fail-safe shutdown. The Packet Ordering Function (POF) solves this by buffering packets and releasing them in the correct sequence.

The POF respects the latency bounds of the DetNet flow: it does not hold packets longer than the flow's deadline allows. Importantly, the POF does not improve reliability—it assumes the PEF has already removed duplicates and does not correct packets that arrive too late.
sections.plainLanguage: When mail arrives by two routes, sometimes the second route gets there first. The POF sorts the mail and hands it over in the right order.

sections.title: How the POF Works
sections.content:
The POF sits between the PEF and the application, acting as a dedicated reordering stage in the DetNet forwarding path. The system tracks sequence numbers on packets (added by the PRF near the source) and uses two main tools: a delay calculator that determines how long to wait, and a conditional delay buffer that holds packets temporarily.

The delay calculator figures out how much buffering time is safe without violating the flow's latency budget. The key insight is that different paths have different delays. If the fastest path has a delay of 10 milliseconds and the slowest has 15 milliseconds, the POF needs to buffer for at most 5 milliseconds to catch out-of-order packets.

The conditional delay buffer only delays packets that arrive out of order. In-order packets flow through without delay. This keeps the system simple and avoids adding unnecessary latency to every packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The POF has a scale: it measures when each packet arrives and how late it is. It has a holding area for late-arriving packets. When the right moment comes, it sends everything in order.

sections.title: The Basic POF Algorithm
sections.content:
The basic algorithm is straightforward. The POF remembers the sequence number of the last packet it sent out (POFLastSent). When a new packet arrives, its sequence number is compared to this value. If the sequence number is the next expected one or earlier (a case handled by other functions), the packet is forwarded immediately and POFLastSent is updated. If the packet's sequence number is higher (meaning it arrived early, ahead of some earlier packet), it goes into the buffer.

Buffered packets wait. They are released when either their turn comes (a packet with a lower sequence number arrives and fills the gap) or a timeout (POFMaxDelay) expires. When POFMaxDelay expires, buffered packets are released even if earlier packets never arrive, because waiting longer would violate the latency bound. The timeout must be at least as large as the delay difference between paths.

Initialization and recovery are simple: if the POF is reset or no packet arrives for a specified time (POFTakeAnyTime), the next packet is treated as in-order, and POFLastSent is updated. This keeps the state minimal and avoids complex synchronization between replication and ordering functions.
sections.plainLanguage: The POF watches the sequence number on each packet and knows which one it sent last. If packet 5 shows up but packet 3 hasn't, packet 5 waits in a holding area. When packet 3 arrives, packet 3 goes out, then packet 4, then packet 5. If nothing arrives for a while, the POF gives up waiting and sends what it has.

sections.title: The Advanced POF Algorithm
sections.content:
In some networks, the remaining latency budget at the POF point is very tight. The basic algorithm might require a POFMaxDelay that is too large to fit within the budget. The advanced algorithm handles this by being aware of which path each packet took.

When a packet arrives, the POF identifies which of the multiple redundant paths it traveled on (using the ingress interface, a FlowID set by the replication function, or other means). Different paths have different delays, so the POF uses different timeout values for different paths (POFMaxDelay_i, where i is the path). Packets on the fastest path can wait longer because they are less likely to be out of order; packets on the slowest path can be released quickly because they represent the last chance to deliver that sequence number.

This refinement allows the POF to respect tighter latency bounds by trading simplicity for precision. Combining the PEF and POF in the same node can simplify path identification, since they already know where packets came from.
sections.plainLanguage: If the holding area is very small, the POF gets smarter. It can wait longer for packets from the fast route (because they are less likely to be out of order) and releases packets from the slow route quickly (because those are probably the last to arrive).

sections.title: Security and Scope
sections.content:
The POF is designed for reordering packets within the latency bound of the flow. It does not provide any additional reliability, duplicate detection, or error correction. Those functions remain the responsibility of the PEF and other DetNet mechanisms. The POF shares the security considerations of the broader PREOF (Packet Replication, Elimination, and Ordering Functions) architecture, which are documented in RFC 9055.

The POF has important limits. It cannot correct packet loss, duplicate packets, or packets that arrive later than the design assumptions permit. If all copies of a packet are lost before reaching the POF, that packet will never arrive. If the network conditions change in ways that violate the assumptions (for example, a path becoming far slower than expected), the POF may deliver out-of-order packets. The algorithm requires engineering: the timeouts and parameters must be set correctly based on the network's path delays and the flow's latency requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The POF only sorts packets it receives. It cannot bring back lost packets or fix scrambled data. If the network is slower than expected, the POF cannot help.
